newsitem.title: UK: RTRS-Canadian gold exploration firms head home.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Canadian gold exploration firms head home.

text.p: Canadian gold exploration firms are returning home after branching out abroad, discovering a huge untapped domestic potential, a geologist told a seminar in London.
"There's been a resurgent emphasis on Canada over the last few years," said Francois Robert, a research scientist with the Geological Survey of Canada.

Firms are finding new types of deposits in traditional mining areas as well as hitting classical types of targets in remote areas which have never been mined before, he said at a seminar sponsored by the Canadian government.
Only 35-40 percent of the vast country has been mapped sufficiently for exploration purposes, Robert said.
Canadian firms have gone increasingly abroad over the past decade, exploring for gold in Latin America, Africa and Asia.

But over the past few years many firms have come home to discover, for example, new deep sulphidic deposits in Canada's traditional mining region of the Abitibi Belt, where quartz vein deposits have been the norm.
One example is the Harker-Holloway area of the Abitibi Belt, where Battle Mountain Gold Co is set to start mining the Lightning Zone mine in May, which is 200-250 metres underground, Robert said.
The mine has reserves of 5.8 million tonnes with 6.7 grams of gold per tonne.
"There's tremendous potential to find new deep discoveries in Abitibi," Robert said.
There is also growing activity in areas which have never seen miners before.
In the Meliadine District of Hudson Bay, not a traditional mining area, two junior firms found quartz vein deposits, he said.
Comaplex Minerals Corp and Cumberland Resources Ltd found 670,000 tonnes at 9.94 grams of gold per tonne at the Discovery site in North West Territories.
Canadian gold production is estimated to have risen last year from 149 tonnes in 1995, but the figures have not been finalised, Robert said.
This is down from a peak in 1991 of nearly 180 tonnes, which matched a similar level in the early 1940s.
